title: A wife at the well (Genesis 24:1–27)
hook: the servant's test: the one who offers water to him and to his camels too

segments.voice: Last week ended with Sarah's burial, and a grave bought at full price. Your line was grief deserves ground. Whose memory did you honor? A new week, and day fifty.

Abraham is old now, and Isaac needs a wife. So Abraham sends his oldest servant on a long journey back to the family's homeland, with ten camels loaded with gifts. The servant arrives outside a town at evening, the hour when the young women come out to draw water. He makes the camels kneel by the well. And he's stuck. How do you pick a person for someone else's whole life? So he prays, in the old JPS translation: "O LORD, the God of my master Abraham, send me, I pray Thee, good speed this day, and show kindness unto my master Abraham." And he sets a test. Not beauty. Not money. Not family name. Something much smaller, and much harder to fake.
screen: `TEN CAMELS AND A LONG ROAD.` → `EVENING AT THE WELL.` → `HOW DO YOU CHOOSE?`

segments.voice: Here's the test. I'll ask a girl for a drink. If she says, drink, and I'll water your camels too, she's the one. And before he's even finished praying, Rebekah comes out with a jar on her shoulder. She fills it. He runs up and asks for a sip. She says, drink, my lord, and hurries to lower the jar. And then, without being asked: "I will draw for thy camels also, until they have done drinking." Stop and picture it. Ten camels, after a desert crossing. A thirsty camel can drink an astonishing amount of water. That's trip after trip down to the spring, jar after jar, for a stranger's animals, in the evening. The Torah says she ran. That's chesed. It's one of the great words of the Hebrew Bible, and it's hard to translate. Kindness. Loving-kindness. Loyal love. Mercy. At its heart, chesed is kindness that goes past what's owed: past fair, past asked. The servant's prayer uses it, show chesed to my master. And when he realizes she's the one, he bows and blesses God, who has not forsaken His mercy, chesed again. The prophet Micah later sums up what God asks of a person: to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly. That mercy is chesed. And the Mishnah says the whole world stands on three things: Torah, worship, and acts of loving-kindness. The servant wasn't looking for someone who'd do what was asked. He was looking for someone who'd notice the camels.
screen: `DRINK, AND YOUR CAMELS TOO.` · `TEN THIRSTY CAMELS.` · `CHESED — KINDNESS PAST WHAT'S OWED.` · `THE WORLD STANDS ON THREE THINGS.` · then, large: `I WILL DRAW FOR THY CAMELS ALSO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think about the requests people make of you in a normal day: pass the salt, send me that file, can you pick up milk. Now think about the camels behind the request. The thing nobody asked for but would make their day lighter. The coworker who asked for the file but is clearly drowning. The parent who asked about dinner but is lonely. Pick one person. Picture the extra thing. If you pray, you can ask to notice. The bell holds the time.
Chesed. Loving-kindness: kindness that goes past what's owed. Rebekah watering ten camels for a stranger.
Your line: water the camels too. Today, offer one kind of help nobody asked you for. Day fifty.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness such as visiting the sick, comforting mourners and helping a bride and groom, among the pillars of Jewish life, and many communities organize them through volunteer groups.

fork.setup: you're at the well at evening. a stranger with ten camels asks you for a sip of water. what do you do?
options: give him a sip and go home.
give him a drink and water all his camels too.
fork.reveal: Rebekah gives him a drink and runs back and forth to water all ten camels until they're done. the servant knows she's the one.

trapdoor: what you thought: chesed means being nice.
what it means: kindness that goes past what's owed, like watering ten camels for a stranger.
what a scholar hears: chesed in the servant's prayer (24:12, 24:14, 24:27), in Micah 6:8's love mercy, and in Pirkei Avot 1:2's acts of loving-kindness.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 24:12 and 24:19.
The servant is unnamed in chapter 24; tradition identifies him as Eliezer (15:2). The script calls him 'his oldest servant' (24:2). Confirm.
'A thirsty camel can drink an astonishing amount' kept vague on purpose (figures of 25–40 gallons are commonly cited).
Micah 6:8 paraphrased ('to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly'), not marked as a JPS quotation; confirm and consider quoting if exact.
Pirkei Avot 1:2 (Simon the Righteous): Torah, avodah, gemilut chasadim. Confirm.
